comments.text: This video reminded me of the Jevons Paradox, based on William S. Jevons assessment during the second industrial revolution, about the idea that Watt's more energy-efficient coal engine would (not) decrease coal price or slow down the coal reserves depletion in GB, because although future engines would become more efficient thanks to Watt's design, the barrier of entry and ongoing cost of machine power would decrease much more significantly, further uplifting demand for coal, which would amplify the cost and resource depletion. While the closest present analogue to this paradox is seen in RAM prices (to the frustration of the consumer market given the price volatility), I see the same point here given for jobs interacting with AI's projected potential, meaning work will not be "hard to come by" given AI, but rather work (and its outputs) will become much more accessible and demanded than before (maybe manifesting in lower prices), but on the caveat that we won't know to which degree wages, work time, or quality of life will improve (or deteriorate) after the fact.

Well concluding from the past onto the future is not really a good argument from my point of view. The question wether human will be replaced by AI cannot really be answered by applying a pattern from the past on current situation. The question is: Is the set of what humans can do replicatable with AI in principle? My answer to that is: yes it is, we are just not there yet. So the solution to the new arising challenge is not: just adapt faster, be better. The solution is to rethink of how our society is structured. The principle of "your worth corresponds to what you can produce" will just be dead soon. We should use the time left to rethink and restructure that principle assigning some basic minimal credit to every member of society and install corresponding wealth redistribution mechanisms
